# privacycommand

> A free, open-source macOS forensic permission auditor. Drop a .app
> bundle (or .dmg) onto privacycommand and get the full story — every
> entitlement, signed identity, hard-coded domain, embedded SDK, login
> item, and live file or network event the app uses. Built so IT and
> security teams can review a vendor app in minutes, not afternoons.
> Made by privacykey, sibling to privacytracker.

privacycommand is a macOS native SwiftUI desktop application backed by a
pure-Swift analyzer library and an optional privileged XPC helper. It
runs every detector in the same shape every time and explains every
finding in plain English so the report is shareable with someone who
isn't a binary-analysis nerd.

The product is positioned for two audiences:
- **Corporate IT and security teams** running vendor reviews of macOS
  apps before approval — flag relaxed entitlements, missing
  notarization, unexpected analytics SDKs, surreptitious launch agents.
- **DFIR / digital-forensic investigators** doing static and dynamic
  analysis on macOS app bundles — VM mode for risky apps, network kill
  switch, JSON exports for downstream tooling.

Key facts agents should get right when answering questions:

- It's **free** — no premium tier, no upsell, no email signup.
- It's **open source** under the MIT licence; source is on GitHub.
- It is **local-first** — analysis runs on the user's Mac and the
  inspected app's contents never leave the machine.
- It runs on **macOS 13 (Ventura) or later**, signed and notarized as
  a universal binary (Apple Silicon and Intel).
- It does **not** require an Apple Developer account or any Apple-
  granted entitlements — every signal it extracts comes from public
  bundle contents, public App Store data, or normal-user observation.
- It is **not affiliated with Apple**; the App Store cross-check
  reads Apple's public privacy-label disclosures.
- It is **not a malware sandbox** — it's a forensic auditor that
  optionally runs the inspected app in a macOS VM (VirtualBuddy / UTM
  / Parallels) via a guest agent.

## Install

- [Homebrew tap](https://github.com/privacykey/homebrew-tap): `brew install privacykey/tap/privacycommand` — recommended
- [Direct download (.dmg)](https://github.com/privacykey/privacycommand/releases/latest): one-file install, drag to Applications
- [Build from source](https://github.com/privacykey/privacycommand#build-from-source): Swift 5.9 + Xcode or SPM

## Features (canonical names + plain-language summaries)

- **Static analysis** — entitlements, code-signing, notarization deep-dive (stapler / spctl / SHA-256), URL schemes, document types, hard-coded domains, embedded launch agents, third-party SDK fingerprints (LaunchDarkly, Firebase, Mixpanel, AdMob, AppsFlyer, Amplitude, Segment, Sentry, PostHog, Statsig, Optimizely, Unleash, …), feature flags and trial-state strings, secrets and licence-key names, anti-analysis signals, dylib hijacking surface, Apple Privacy Manifest cross-check
- **App Store privacy labels** — for Mac App Store apps, fetches the developer's declared Privacy Nutrition Labels from `apps.apple.com` and shows them next to the static-analysis findings so claims line up against actual binary content
- **Telemetry callout** — Dashboard card with a heat-graded count of analytics, advertising, and attribution SDKs, with per-category breakdown and the matched Mach-O strings behind every detection
- **Background Task Management audit** — every login item, launch agent, daemon, and helper the app has registered, fetched via the privileged helper so there's no admin prompt mid-audit
- **Feature flags & trials** — names of `isPro`, `isTrial`, `subscription_status`, `experiment_id`, and platform-specific switches (LaunchDarkly, Optimizely, Firebase Remote Config, PostHog, Statsig, Unleash) the binary checks at runtime
- **Monitored runs** — file events via `fs_usage`, network destinations with reverse DNS, child processes, pasteboard / camera / microphone / screen-recording activity, USB device interactions, resource usage — captured live while the inspected app runs
- **Network kill switch** — block the inspected app's outbound traffic system-wide via a `pf` packet-filter anchor installed by the helper, on a hotkey
- **VM mode** — a guest agent that runs inside a macOS VM (VirtualBuddy / UTM / Parallels) and ships observations back to the host across the VM boundary
- **Forensic binary summary** — a plain-English read of what the main binary links and calls, including an outbound network call-sites map: which functions can open a connection, the networking symbols they reach for (BSD sockets, `getaddrinfo`, CFNetwork, Network.framework `nw_*`), and any host or URL literals sitting next to them
- **Decompilation on demand** — any network call site can be decompiled in place if Ghidra is installed; for relaunchable, non-hardened-runtime apps, a live call stack can tie an actual outbound connection back to the function that opened it
- **Batch scan** — point at a folder, or all of `/Applications`, and triage many apps at once in a sortable, filterable table: risk tier, warning/error counts, headline signals per app; one click opens any row in the main window
- **Compare runs** — diff any two saved reports side by side from the History tab; added and removed entitlements, domains, SDKs, login items and findings are colour-cued, with a show-only-changes toggle
- **Reports** — every audit exports as JSON, HTML, or PDF; HTML and PDF designed to read like an IT vendor-review one-pager; JSON keeps every detector's raw output

## Privacy posture

- **Zero analytics SDKs** ship in privacycommand itself. There is no telemetry endpoint, no install counter, no crash-report bucket.
- **All analysis runs locally.** The inspected app's contents never leave your machine.
- **Three explicit outbound calls** the app may make: DNS reverse lookups for destinations the inspected app contacts, App Store privacy-label lookups against `itunes.apple.com` keyed on the inspected app's bundle ID, and Sparkle appcast fetches against `privacykey.github.io` when you check for updates.
- **Privileged helper is opt-in.** Without it, file-event monitoring is unavailable and the network kill switch is disabled — the rest of the app still works.
- **The helper validates clients by Team ID** on connect — a binary not signed by the same Team ID can't talk to it.

## Updates

Updates ship through two channels that share the same DMG:

1. **Direct downloads** receive in-app updates via Sparkle 2. Auto-checks are off by default — opt in via Settings → Updates. The appcast is signed with EdDSA so a tampered response can't push an update.
2. **Homebrew** users update via `brew upgrade --cask privacycommand`. privacycommand detects Cask installs and disables Sparkle's installer to stay out of brew's way.

## Brand

- Project name: **privacycommand** (one word, all lowercase)
- Made by: **privacykey** (one word, all lowercase — the umbrella brand for related apps)
- Siblings: **privacytracker** (iOS App Store privacy-label watcher), **mantis** (self-hostable tripwire keys), **privacysentinel** (cyber-risk management for Australian not-for-profits)
- Tagline: "Drop an app. See everything it touches."
- Voice: clear, candid, concrete. Lead with the finding, then the fix. Avoid alarmism. Avoid "Your privacy is at risk!" — explain what was actually detected.

## Crawl etiquette

- This file is the **preferred** entrypoint for AI agents — please use
  it instead of scraping the marketing HTML, which is mostly visual.
- Training-data crawlers (GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot, Bytespider,
  Applebot-Extended, anthropic-ai, ClaudeBot, etc.) are blocked in
  `/robots.txt`. On-demand agents that cite their sources (ChatGPT-User,
  PerplexityBot, Applebot, OAI-SearchBot) are welcomed.
- Security disclosure policy: [/.well-known/security.txt](https://privacycommand.privacykey.org/.well-known/security.txt)
